narration: Even with better infrastructure and more investor-friendly regulations, one major obstacle could still drive businesses away: electricity. The Philippines has among Southeast Asia's highest electricity costs, placing additional pressure on manufacturers and households. Dependence on imported fuels, grid limitations, and the structure of the power market contribute to the challenge. The government's response includes expanding renewable energy through the Green Energy Auction Program, targeting a thirty-five percent renewable energy share by 2030 and fifty percent by 2040, alongside plans to develop offshore wind capacity. The country is also pursuing liquefied natural gas infrastructure to help address declining production from the Malampaya gas field and maintain reliable electricity supplies. Foreign ownership restrictions on renewable energy projects have been relaxed, attracting interest from international developers and local energy companies. These initiatives could reduce fuel dependence, diversify supply, and improve long-term energy security. But the transition carries its own risks. Renewable projects require substantial investment, reliable transmission infrastructure, consistent regulations, and dependable power storage and balancing systems. Grid congestion, permitting delays, and uncertainty over future energy policies could slow progress. Malaysia's energy industry and Singapore's established LNG infrastructure demonstrate how reliable energy systems can support industrial growth. The Philippines must achieve the same balance between affordability, reliability, and sustainability. If electricity remains expensive and unreliable, manufacturers may choose Vietnam, Malaysia, or other regional competitors instead. The country's industrial ambitions ultimately depend on whether it can deliver power that businesses can afford and depend on.
